label: Tehillim (Psalms) — Part 5 — Psalms 90–106
summary_plain: Psalms 90 through 106 open with the only psalm attributed to Moshe: YHWH, you have been our dwelling place in all generations. Before the mountains were brought forth, from everlasting to everlasting, you are El. Psalm 91 promises shelter under the wings of the Most High. Psalm 100 calls all the earth to serve YHWH with gladness. Psalm 103 declares YHWH's compassion: as far as the east is from the west, so far does he remove our transgressions. Psalm 104 is the great creation hymn — YHWH stretches out the heavens like a tent, makes the clouds his chariot, rides on the wings of the wind. Psalm 106 recounts the covenant history from Mitzrayim through the wilderness to the land.
summary_scholarly: The ACR reads Psalms 90-106 from DSS witnesses and the Orit Ge'ez. Psalm 90 is attributed to Moshe — the only psalm with this attribution — connecting the Tehillim to the Torah itself. Psalm 104 has long been compared to the Egyptian Great Hymn to the Aten (c. 1350 BCE), attributed to Akhenaten. Both texts praise the creator for the orderly provision of the natural world in strikingly parallel language. This is not borrowing but shared inheritance — both emerge from the same Afro-Asiatic intellectual tradition. The ACR places these texts in conversation. Psalm 104 is Hebrew praise; the Hymn to the Aten is Egyptian praise. Both come from the African continent's monotheistic impulse. The DSS fragments preserve variant readings in Psalm 104 and throughout this section that demonstrate the Masoretic is not the original form.

key_terms.term: Psalm 110 Sit at My Right Hand
key_terms.definition: 'YHWH says to my lord: Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool.' Ancient source text; NT writers borrowed more from Psalm 110 than any other psalm in Tehillim — it is the most cited ancient text in the NT. The direction is ancient text → NT, not prophecy fulfilled.

'You are a priest forever after the order of Malkhi-Tzedek.' YHWH's oath establishing the anointed king as a priest in the line of the ancient Malkhi-Tzedek figure from Bereshit 14. Ancient source; NT writers borrowed this for the high-priesthood claims in the letter to the Hebrews.

'The stone that the builders rejected has become the cornerstone.' Ancient wisdom about unexpected reversal — what human builders discarded, YHWH made the foundation. NT writers borrowed this extensively.

'Hoshiana! Save us now, O YHWH! O YHWH, please grant us success!' A cry of appeal and acclamation at the festival procession. Ancient source; NT writers borrowed 'Hosanna' directly from this Psalm 118 cry.

The longest psalm and the longest chapter in the Hebrew scriptures: 176 verses in 22 stanzas, each stanza corresponding to a letter of the Hebrew aleph-bet. All eight verses in each stanza contain one of eight synonyms for YHWH's Torah/instruction.
'Your word is a lamp to my feet and a light to my path.' YHWH's Torah as the guide through darkness — not distant or theoretical but immediately practical for each step.

Fifteen psalms (Ps.120-134) carrying the superscription 'A Song of Ascents' — pilgrim songs sung while ascending to Yerushalayim for the three festivals. Their brevity and memorable nature suited the journey.

Several psalms use the Hebrew aleph-bet as an organizing structure: each verse or stanza begins with the next letter. Besides Psalm 119 (the longest), Psalms 9-10, 25, 34, 37, 111, 112, and 145 also use acrostic forms.

key_terms.term: This Is the Day YHWH Made (118:24)
key_terms.definition: 'This is the day that YHWH has made; let us rejoice and be glad in it.' A liturgical acclamation at YHWH's saving act — the specific 'day' in context is the day of rescue from affliction referenced throughout Psalm 118.

Psalm 136, which repeats 'for his steadfast love endures forever' (ki le'olam khasdo) after every one of its 26 verses. Called the Great Hallel to distinguish it from the Egyptian Hallel (Ps.113-118). Used at Pesakh and Shabbat.

faq.question: Why is Psalm 110 called the most-cited psalm in the NT?
faq.answer: NT writers borrowed from Psalm 110 more than from any other single psalm: 'Sit at my right hand' appears in multiple NT narratives and letters, 'the order of Malkhi-Tzedek' is the foundation of the entire priesthood argument in the Letter to the Hebrews, and 'until I make your enemies your footstool' recurs throughout NT polemic. All of this material is ancient. The NT is the borrower; Psalm 110 is the ancient source text.

faq.question: What is the Malkhi-Tzedek priesthood order in Psalm 110:4?
faq.answer: Malkhi-Tzedek ('king of righteousness') appears in Bereshit 14:18-20 as the king-priest of Shalem who blessed Avraham and received a tenth from him. Psalm 110:4 uses this ancient figure to describe a combined royal-priestly role for YHWH's anointed — priest and king, not through Levitical descent but through YHWH's own oath. This ancient Hebrew royal-priestly concept was borrowed wholesale by NT writers for their invented figure's role in Hebrews.

faq.question: What does Psalm 118's 'stone the builders rejected' mean in its original context?
faq.answer: Psalm 118 is a liturgical thanksgiving for YHWH's rescue from great affliction and near-death. The 'stone the builders rejected' is the psalmist/community that was dismissed and overlooked by the powerful, only to be vindicated by YHWH as foundational. The image is about unexpected reversal — the discarded becomes central. NT writers borrowed this for their crucifixion/resurrection narrative. The original is about covenant vindication, not a person.

faq.question: What is Psalm 119 and why was it composed as an acrostic?
faq.answer: Psalm 119 is 176 verses organized as 22 stanzas of 8 verses each, with every stanza assigned to a successive letter of the aleph-bet. Every verse in a stanza uses words beginning with that letter. Additionally, every verse contains at least one of eight synonyms for YHWH's instruction (Torah, edot, piqqudim, khuqqim, mishpatim, mitzvot, devarim, 'imrot). The acrostic form communicates that praise of YHWH's Torah covers everything — from aleph to tav, the whole scope of existence.

faq.question: What does 'your word is a lamp to my feet' mean in Psalm 119:105?
faq.answer: The image is of walking in darkness with only a lamp — YHWH's word illuminates not the whole landscape at once but the immediate next step. It is practical covenant guidance for each moment, not abstract theological knowledge. The lamp metaphor emphasizes the lived, daily dependence on YHWH's instruction for navigating specific decisions, not just general principles.

faq.question: What are the Songs of Ascent and how were they used?
faq.answer: The 15 Songs of Ascent (Ps.120-134) were pilgrim psalms sung while ascending to Yerushalayim for the three annual festivals — Pesakh, Shavuot, and Sukkot. The 'ascent' refers both to the physical ascent up to Yerushalayim (which sits at elevation) and to the liturgical procession. Their brevity, memorable refrains, and community focus made them suitable for group singing on the journey.

faq.question: What is the Great Hallel (Psalm 136) and how is it structured?
faq.answer: Psalm 136 is called the Great Hallel — 26 verses each ending with the identical refrain: 'for his steadfast love endures forever' (ki le'olam khasdo). The first verses praise YHWH as Creator; the middle verses recount the Exodus and wilderness; the later verses thank YHWH for deliverance and provision. The unvarying refrain trains the community to anchor every act of YHWH in the same bedrock truth: loyal covenant love that does not end.

faq.question: How does Psalm 107 open Book V of Tehillim?
faq.answer: Psalm 107 opens Book V with four scenes of rescue — lost travelers found by YHWH, prisoners freed, the sick healed, sailors saved from storm. Each ends with the same refrain: 'Let them thank YHWH for his steadfast love, for his wondrous works to the children of man.' Book V begins with a universal call to give thanks to the rescuing YHWH, connecting to the exile and return experience of the whole community.

faq.question: Why does Psalm 110 describe the anointed as both king and priest?
faq.answer: In standard Hebrew practice, the roles of king and priest were separate — the king from Yehudah/David, the priests from Levi/Aaron. Psalm 110 describes an anointed figure who holds both roles, legitimated not by lineage but by YHWH's direct oath ('YHWH has sworn and will not change his mind'). This models the ancient pre-Levitical royal-priestly figure Malkhi-Tzedek as the template for a new kind of combined authority directly from YHWH.

faq.question: What makes Psalm 119 unique as a Torah psalm?
faq.answer: Psalm 119 is entirely devoted to praising and meditating on YHWH's Torah — no plea for military victory, no historical recital, no lament about enemies primarily. Its 176 verses explore every angle of the covenant person's relationship to YHWH's instruction: loving it, being afflicted and comforted by it, being guided by it, longing for it when persecuted, treasuring it above wealth. It is the Psalter's fullest statement that YHWH's Torah is not a burden but a delight.
